identification.summary: Financially motivated cybercriminal actor that Microsoft describes as both an access broker focused on malware distribution through search advertisements and an 'as-a-service' provider of malicious installers and landing-page frameworks [S1]. Microsoft identifies Storm-1113 as the developer of EugenLoader, a commodity loader delivered as a malicious MSIX installer [S1]. CrowdStrike tracks APOTHECARY SPIDER, which it says develops and rents EugenLoader and advertises it on underground forums [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft observed Storm-1113's EugenLoader delivered through search ads mimicking Zoom since mid-November 2023 [S1]. Microsoft cites EugenLoader as first observed around November 2022 [S1]. CrowdStrike states APOTHECARY SPIDER has been active since at least March 2021 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1113 (development-stage designation, no volcanic or weather family name in sources gathered). EugenLoader is also tracked as FakeBat, NUMOZYLOD and PaykLoader [S3]; Mandiant attributes the NUMOZYLOD malware-as-a-service operation to UNC4536 [S3]. The sources gathered do not state that UNC4536, Eugenfest and Storm-1113 are the same cluster; treat the overlap as unverified. Alias mapping Storm-1113 to APOTHECARY SPIDER is from Microsoft's naming mapping [S6].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor. Microsoft classifies Storm-1113 as a financially motivated actor [S1][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes the role and tooling directly (developer of EugenLoader, access broker, as-a-service provider) [S1]. No government attribution found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and reporting on App Installer abuse [S1]; CrowdStrike adversary profile of APOTHECARY SPIDER [S2]; Microsoft naming mapping [S6].

objectives: Financial gain through selling or renting loader and landing-page services and malware distribution, which feeds follow-on payloads such as stealers, RATs and loaders operated by other criminals [S1][S2].

targeting.notes: Victims are opportunistic: users searching for popular software (Zoom lures in Microsoft's reporting) [S1]. Mandiant-reported FakeBat/NUMOZYLOD lures impersonate Brave, KeePass, Notion, Steam and Zoom [S3]. No sector or regional focus is stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: EugenLoader is a malicious MSIX installer that is downloaded on a device and used to deliver additional payloads; Microsoft names Gozi, Redline stealer, IcedID, Smoke Loader, NetSupport Manager, Sectop RAT and Lumma stealer among payloads seen with Storm-1113 activity [S1]. Storm-1113 supplies installers and landing-page frameworks that other actors reuse, including Sangria Tempest (FIN7) and Storm-1674 [S1]. Microsoft detects the loader as TrojanDownloader:PowerShell/EugenLoader and Trojan:Win32/EugenLoader [S1]; Microsoft Security Intelligence describes a loader that fetches an encrypted GPG file and decrypts it locally, with likely payloads Bumblebee or IcedID [S5]. Mandiant reporting on the same loader family notes MSIX packages with a startScript configuration that runs a script before the legitimate app launches, and host profiling (OS, domain, antivirus, public IP addresses) before payload delivery [S3]. Critical Start reported a June 2024 variant it calls IvanLoader that uses Telegram bots to receive commands [S4].

campaigns.name: EugenLoader first observed
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cites EugenLoader as a commodity malware first observed around November 2022.

campaigns.name: Zoom-themed search-ad delivery of EugenLoader
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Storm-1113's EugenLoader delivered through search advertisements mimicking the Zoom app, using the ms-appinstaller protocol since mid-November 2023.

campaigns.name: Sangria Tempest (FIN7) use of EugenLoader
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Sangria Tempest using Storm-1113's EugenLoader via malicious MSIX installs, dropping Carbanak and then Gracewire.

campaigns.name: Storm-1674 use of Storm-1113 installers and frameworks
campaigns.summary: Storm-1674 used Teams messages with spoofed SharePoint/OneDrive pages invoking ms-appinstaller, likely dropping SectopRAT or DarkGate via Storm-1113 installers and frameworks.

campaigns.name: Microsoft disables ms-appinstaller handler
campaigns.summary: Microsoft disabled the ms-appinstaller protocol handler by default (App Installer build 1.21.3421.0) in response to abuse by Storm-1113 and other actors.

campaigns.name: IvanLoader variant of FakeBat/EugenLoader
campaigns.summary: Critical Start reported a new variant it calls IvanLoader, a variant of FakeBat (EugenLoader), using Telegram bots for commands.

campaigns.name: Mandiant reporting on FakeBat/NUMOZYLOD malvertising (UNC4536)
campaigns.summary: Coverage of Mandiant reporting describes malvertising via typosquatted sites hosting trojanized MSIX installers of Brave, KeePass, Notion, Steam and Zoom, with payloads including Carbanak, IcedID, Lumma, RedLine and SectopRAT. Cluster link to Storm-1113 not stated in this source.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated developer and service provider of EugenLoader; tracked as Storm-1113 (Microsoft) and APOTHECARY SPIDER (CrowdStrike) [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.capability: EugenLoader MSIX loader, malicious installers, landing-page frameworks, ms-appinstaller abuse [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Search-advertisement placements and fake software landing pages [S1]; underground forum advertising of the loader [S2]; Telegram bot command channel in a reported variant [S4].
diamond.victim: Users searching for popular software such as Zoom; downstream victims of customers including Sangria Tempest (FIN7) and Storm-1674 [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime-as-a-service economy in which loader developers sell or rent access paths to ransomware and data-theft operators [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows MSIX/App Installer packaging and the ms-appinstaller protocol handler, search advertising platforms, and user trust in software download sites [S1].

gaps: Overlap among Storm-1113, UNC4536 (Mandiant), Eugenfest and APOTHECARY SPIDER is not confirmed by the sources opened; only Microsoft's mapping to APOTHECARY SPIDER was used [S3][S6].
CrowdStrike's APOTHECARY SPIDER page could not be fetched directly; its content is taken from search-result excerpts [S2].
Microsoft's primary blog was read in full via fetch, but Storm-1113 activity after December 2023 is not documented in Microsoft sources gathered.
No victim counts, sectors, geography or financial figures are available for Storm-1113 itself.
The Malpedia EugenLoader entry and eSentire's 2023-12-12 'Unraveling BatLoader and FakeBat' report were seen only as search references and not opened.
No law-enforcement action, indictment or sanction was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user workstation download path: search engines, software-download sites, and the Windows App Installer and MSIX handling that Storm-1113 abuses [S1]. STEP 2: This is a commodity enabler, not a state actor; its customers include FIN7 and Teams-phishing access brokers who hand off to ransomware operators [S1]. STEP 3: Typical chain is a search ad or fake software page, then a malicious MSIX installer (EugenLoader), then a stealer, RAT or loader such as Carbanak, SectopRAT, DarkGate or IcedID [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic malvertising against users on any network, including DoD-adjacent personnel using unmanaged or personal devices, yielding credential theft and access for resale. MDCOA is a customer selling or using such access against a defense contractor or installation network to stage ransomware or data theft. Candidate indicators: ms-appinstaller or MSIX installs from web downloads, PowerShell spawned by MSIX packages with startScript behavior, detections named EugenLoader, and outbound Telegram bot traffic from workstations [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track commodity loader activity as an early indicator of access sales, since multiple downstream actors share the same installers [S1]. (2) Authorities: application control and App Installer policy changes on DoDIN endpoints fall to network owners and the supporting cyber defense service provider; confirm the ms-appinstaller handler is disabled on patched App Installer builds [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize endpoint controls (SmartScreen, PUA blocking, attack surface reduction) and software-source whitelisting for mission-critical enclaves [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and DIB partners, and brief users on typosquatted software sites and sponsored search results [S1][S3].
